name: Cato Ouyang
bio: Cato Ouyang (born 1993; earlier exhibited as Catalina Ouyang) was born in Chicago and lives in New York. They hold an MFA in sculpture from Yale. Their sculptures join hand-carved stone and wood to found furniture, plaster, papier-mâché, animal bone, horse hair, textiles and, in earlier works, living cultures of bacteria and yeast. Many pieces retell stories from classical myth, literature, art history and family history, and deal with trauma, grief, the body and transformation. The Terrarium works (2017) are lotus feet, imagined from the artist's great-grandmother's bound feet, carved from stone. Ouyang has had solo exhibitions at Knockdown Center, New York (2020), Real Art Ways, Hartford (2021), Night Gallery, Los Angeles (forgive everything, 2022) and three at Lyles & King, New York; the last, Trick (2024), was named one of Artforum's top ten shows of that year. Their work is in collections including the Brooklyn Museum, LACMA, the Nasher Sculpture Center and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
studyNotes: Carve some parts, find the rest. A hand-carved limb or head sits on a school desk, a display case or an abandoned chair; the labour of carving is set against objects that arrive already loaded with use.
Let furniture stand in for bodies. Chairs, drawers and desks are given legs, spines and wounds, so ordinary domestic forms carry the figure without a full figurative sculpture.

Retell an old story from a different side. Titles name Perseus, Lucretia, Lamia and Thérèse; the work picks up stories in which women are attacked, punished or looked at, and shifts who holds the power in them.
Mix the stable with the perishable. Marble and soapstone share space with raw egg, kombucha mothers and beeswax, so the sculpture contains both permanence and decay.
Write the title as part of the work. Long, poetic titles and parentheses, such as crisis management (P[erseus] came for the holes), add a voice the objects alone could not carry.
Move between sculpture and moving image. Videos such as Syzygy use motors, scrims and directional sound, treating projection as another sculptural material.
